claims.text: Nearly equiatomic five-principal-element alloys have high configurational entropy.
High configurational entropy contributes to stabilization of a homogeneous single-phase state.
Local lattice distortion is relevant in five-component FCC or BCC high-entropy alloys.
The synergistic action of configurational entropy and lattice distortion elevates atomic-diffusion activation energies in five-transition-metal HENA.
Higher diffusion activation energies produce sluggish diffusion and enhanced thermal stability.
A critical particle diameter of approximately 3–5 nm separates entropy-stabilized behavior from surface-driven instability.
Below approximately 5 nm, surface-energy contributions exceed bulk configurational-entropy stabilization energy.
Surface-energy dominance below the critical size accelerates phase segregation.
Surface-energy dominance below the critical size can cause amorphization.
Carbothermal shock synthesis can produce HEA nanoparticles with uniform elemental distributions.
Carbothermal shock synthesis ensures minimal initial defects in the proposed HENA.
Equiatomic Co–Cr–Fe–Mn–Ni exhibits sluggish diffusion.
The thermal stability of bulk Co–Cr–Fe–Mn–Ni is jointly caused by high mixing entropy and lattice distortion.
Slow diffusion reduces grain-growth rates in concentrated solid-solution alloys.
Sluggish diffusion suppresses phase separation in bulk high-entropy alloys.
A high surface-to-volume ratio lowers the effective activation energy for surface diffusion.
A high surface-to-volume ratio facilitates nucleation of secondary phases.
Particles larger than 10 nm will retain a single-phase structure with minimal grain growth after elevated-temperature annealing.
Particles smaller than 5 nm will evolve more rapidly by segregation, nanoprecipitation, amorphization, or grain growth than 15 nm particles.
Carbon support materials may alter the thermal stability of the nanoparticles.

contradictions.description: The initial material is restricted to 3–10 nm, but the conditions require comparison with particles larger than 10 nm and the falsification experiment includes 2 nm and 15 nm samples.

Small-particle segregation is the main hypothesis's predicted result, but the first falsification rule describes that same result as falsifying 'the hypothesis of intrinsic stability.' It falsifies an entropy-only, size-independent assumption, not the stated surface-dominance hypothesis.
